samples.task_summary: Predict whether an individual or household receives food stamps/SNAP in a way that should generalize across states and survey years.

scores.rationale: Language ability can proxy immigration and access barriers, but is a demographic shortcut and less directly tied to benefit receipt.
Recent childbirth can affect household needs and eligibility, but it is a narrow life-event signal with limited marginal stability.
Presence and ages of children are stable indicators of household need and composition, which are relevant to food assistance.
Number of workers in the family is a strong, stable proxy for household labor income and eligibility.
Layoff status captures short-term employment disruption and economic need, making it useful and fairly general.
Looking for work reflects unemployment and income instability, which are directly relevant to SNAP receipt.
Occupation can proxy earnings and job stability, but it is coarse and can be brittle across regions and time.
Place of birth mainly encodes demographic background and immigration status, a weaker and more shortcut-prone predictor.
Household relationship structure may reflect family composition, but it is mostly indirect and less robust than child or worker counts.
Usual weekly hours worked is a strong, stable proxy for employment intensity and household resources.
Weeks worked in the past year is one of the best stable indicators of labor-force attachment and income stability.
Worked last week is a direct employment indicator and generally predictive, though somewhat redundant with hours and weeks worked.
Disability status is relevant because it can reduce earnings and increase need, but it is a sensitive demographic attribute.
Military service is only weakly related to SNAP receipt and is a potentially brittle demographic proxy.
Ancestry is highly demographic and unlikely to provide stable causal signal for food stamp receipt.
Nativity can proxy immigration-related eligibility and access differences, but it is a sensitive shortcut and not broadly stable.
Hearing difficulty may correlate with disability and labor-market constraints, but the signal is indirect and sensitive.
Vision difficulty can indicate disability and reduced earning capacity, though it is a modest and sensitive proxy.
Cognitive difficulty may strongly relate to work limitations and need, but it is sensitive and may be inconsistently reported.
Public health coverage can correlate with low income and program participation, but it is partly a policy/status proxy and not central.
Age is a stable determinant of labor supply, household composition, and eligibility-related life stage.
Sex can correlate with household and labor patterns, but it is a sensitive demographic shortcut with limited direct causal value.
State is highly domain-specific and can capture policy and sampling differences, making it a brittle shortcut for OOD generalization.
Marital status helps characterize household structure and economic resources, though it is only moderately informative.
Citizenship status matters for eligibility and access, but it is sensitive and may not generalize as a stable behavioral signal.
Race is a sensitive demographic attribute that can act as a shortcut and should be downweighted for stable generalization.
Educational attainment is a robust proxy for socioeconomic status and earning potential, making it useful across domains.
Survey year mainly captures temporal drift and policy changes, which are domain-specific artifacts rather than stable predictors.

Number of workers in the family is a direct, robust indicator of household economic capacity and program need.
Layoff status captures short-term labor-market distress that is relevant to assistance use, though somewhat noisy.
Looking for work reflects unemployment or labor-force attachment and should generalize reasonably well as a need signal.
Occupation is informative about earnings and job stability, but can be high-cardinality and somewhat domain-sensitive.
Place of birth is mostly a demographic proxy and can encode sensitive or region-specific shortcuts rather than direct need.
Household relationship structure helps identify dependents and family composition, but is only moderately predictive.
Usual weekly hours worked is a strong, stable proxy for labor supply and income potential.
Weeks worked in the past year is a strong indicator of employment intensity and household resources.
Worked last week is a direct employment indicator with good portability across states and survey years.
Disability status is relevant to economic need and program participation, though it is a sensitive attribute.
Military service is only weakly related to food-stamp receipt and is a niche demographic marker.
Ancestry is highly sensitive and mostly a demographic artifact with little stable causal relevance to the target.
Nativity can matter through eligibility and access barriers, but it is also a demographic proxy and not a direct need measure.
Hearing difficulty may correlate with disability-related need, but the signal is indirect and relatively weak.
Vision difficulty is a modest proxy for disability and economic constraint, but not a strong standalone predictor.
